title: Definition
body_md:
A {\it Hamiltonian path\/} in a graph is a subgraph that is a path graph and
contains all vertices of the original graph.
A {\it Hamiltonian cycle\/} in a graph is a subgraph that is a cycle graph and
contains all vertices of the original graph.
A {\it directed Hamiltonian path [cycle]\/} is a Hamiltonian path [cycle] with directed edges
such that each vertex is the start of one edge and the end of another.
head: environment

label: thm:Hpath
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every Hamiltonian path in the complete multipartite graph has consecutive vertices in different partite subsets,
since no two vertices in the same partite subset are connected by an edge.
It therefore corresponds to a
linear arrangement of $|V_1|, |V_2|, \dots, |V_m|$ otherwise indistinguishable
blocks of colour $1, 2, \dots, m$, respectively, such that no two consecutive
blocks share the same colour, and further an allocation of the $|V_j|$ vertices
in partite subset $V_j$ to the $|V_j|$ blocks of colour $j$.
There are $e_{(|V_1|, |V_2|, \dots, |V_m|)}$ different linear arrangements of
the blocks, and the number of different assignments of $|V_j|$ vertex labels
for colour $j$ is equal to $|V_j|!$, giving Equation (\ref{Thm2.2}) in
total.
head: environment

label: lem:E
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:E}
Let $m\in\mathbb N$, $m\ge 2$, and $n \in \mathbb N^m$. Then
$$
\tilde E_n = {|n| \choose n} \left(1 - \frac{\sum_{j=1}^m n_j\,(n_j-1)}{|n|\,(|n| - 1)} \right).
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We calculate $\tilde E_n$ by subtracting from the number of all different
linear arrangements the number of those arrangements that start and end with
an object of the same colour. For colour $j$, we place one object of this
colour at the beginning and one at the end of the line. (This presupposes
$n_j \ge 2$; otherwise there clearly is no linear arrangement both starting
and ending with an object of colour $j$.)
The remaining objects are placed between them in an unconstrained linear
arrangement of length $|n| - 2$, with only $n_j - 2$ objects of colour $j$.
Doing this for all colours, we find
\begin{align*}
\tilde E_n &= {|n| \choose n} - \sum_{j\in\{1, \dots, m\}, n_j > 1} {|n| - 2 \choose n_1, \dots, n_{j-1}, n_j - 2, n_{j+1}, \dots, n_m}
\\
&= {|n| \choose n} - \frac{(|n| - 2)!}{n_1!\,n_2!\,\cdots\,n_m!} \sum_{j\in\{1, \dots, m\}, n_j > 1} \frac{n_j!}{(n_j - 2)!}
\\
&= {|n| \choose n} \left(1 - \frac{(|n| - 2)!}{|n|!} \sum_{j\in\{1, \dots, m\}, n_j > 1} \frac{n_j!}{(n_j - 2)!} \right)
\\
&= {|n| \choose n} \left(1 - \frac{1}{|n|\,(|n| - 1)} \sum_{j=1}^m n_j\,(n_j - 1) \right).
\qedhere
\end{align*}

title: Remark
head: environment

label: thm:Ee
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First consider the linear arrangements of $n_1, \dots, n_m$ objects of colours
$1, \dots, m$, for general $n \in\mathbb N^m$, only under the constraint that
the first and last objects have different colours.
The number of such arrangements is $\tilde E_n$, given in Lemma \ref{lem:E}.
When we collapse such an arrangement by replacing every consecutive chain of
objects of the same colour by a single object of that colour, we obtain a
linear arrangement of (fewer) objects that satisfies the conditions that no
two adjacent objects have the same colour and that the first and last objects
have different colours.
If the collapsed arrangement has $k_j$ objects of colour $j$, then there are
${n - 1_m \choose k - 1_m}$ different ways this collapsed line can have arisen
from an original arrangement of $n_1, \dots, n_m$ objects; indeed, the
assignment of $n_j$ objects to $k_j$ collapsed objects is equivalent to
placing $k_j-1$ dividers in the $n_j - 1$ spaces between the $n_j$ objects.

We thus obtain the equation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Ee}
\tilde E_n = \sum_{1_m \le k \le n} {n - 1_m \choose k - 1_m} \tilde e_k.
\end{equation}
Now we use the multivariate power series
\begin{equation*}
\exp\left(\pm\sum_{j=1}^m x_j \right) = \sum_{l \in \mathbb N_0^m} (\pm 1)^{|l|} \frac{x^l}{l!}
\qquad (x = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_m) \in \mathbb C^m)
\end{equation*}
and the Cauchy product formula to write the generating function for
$\tilde e_k$ as follows,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{k \in {\mathbb N}_0^m} \tilde e_{1_m+k}\,\frac{x^k}{k!}
 &= \left(\sum_{k \in {\mathbb N}_0^m} \tilde e_{1_m+k}\,\frac{x^k}{k!} \right)
  \left(\sum_{l \in {\mathbb N}_0^m} \frac{x^l}{l!} \right)
  \left(\sum_{l \in {\mathbb N}_0^m} (-1)^{|l|} \frac{x^l}{l!} \right)
\\
 &= \left(\sum_{n \in {\mathbb N}_0^m} \left(\sum_{0_m \le k \le n} \frac{\tilde e_{1_m+k}}{k! (n-k)!} \right) x^n \right)
  \left(\sum_{l \in {\mathbb N}_0^m} (-1)^{|l|} \frac{x^l}{l!} \right)
\\
 &= \left(\sum_{n \in {\mathbb N}_0^m} \left(\sum_{0_m \le k \le n} {n \choose k} \tilde e_{1_m+k} \right) \frac{x^n}{n!} \right)
  \left(\sum_{l \in {\mathbb N}_0^m} (-1)^{|l|} \frac{x^l}{l!} \right)
\\
 &= \left(\sum_{n \in {\mathbb N}_0^m} \tilde E_{n + 1_m} \frac{x^n}{n!} \right)
  \left(\sum_{l \in {\mathbb N}_0^m} (-1)^{|l|} \frac{x^l}{l!} \right)
\\
 &= \sum_{k \in {\mathbb N}_0^m} \left(\sum_{0_m \le l \le k} (-1)^{|l|}\,\frac{k!}{l! (k-l)!}\,\tilde E_{1_m+k-l} \right) \frac{x^k}{k!}.
\end{align*}
(Note that the power series defining the generating function is convergent for
all $x\in\mathbb C^m$) as $\tilde e_{1_m + k} \le e_{1_m + k}$ and the
series for the generating function of the latter was shown to be convergent in
\cite{LSDF&NSS}.)
Hence we can read off
\begin{equation*}
\tilde e_{1_m + k} = \sum_{0_m \le l \le k} (-1)^{|k|} {k \choose l} \tilde E_{1_m + k - l},
\end{equation*}
which gives the identity stated in the theorem.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The proof in \cite{LSDF&NSS} is fully analogous to the above, with the difference that the left-hand side in
equation (\ref{eq:Ee}) is replaced with the count of
unconstrained linear arrangements, i.e.\ the multinomial ${|n| \choose n}$.
This suggests that the collapsing argument used here may be applicable to
other situations where a colour non-adjacency condition is to be introduced
into a counting argument.
head: environment

label: thm:cyc
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cyc}
The number of directed Hamiltonian cycles in the complete multipartite graph
$K_{V_1, V_2, \dots, V_m}$ is equal to
$$
 H^C(K_{V_1, V_2, \dots, V_m}) = \tilde e_{(|V_1|, |V_2|, \dots, |V_m|)}\,
 \frac{\prod_{j=1}^m |V_j|!}{|V|}\,.
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every directed Hamiltonian cycle gives rise to $|V|$ different directed
Hamiltonian paths with the property that the start and end vertex lie in
different partite subsets; therefore we can reduce the question to counting
the latter.
In analogy to the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:Hpath}, we observe that any such
Hamiltonian path corresponds to a linear arrangement of coloured blocks as
in counting problem CP2 and subsequent assignment of vertices in each
partite subset to blocks of the corresponding colour, so there are
$\tilde e_{(|V_1|, |V_2|, \dots, |V_m|)} \prod_{j=1}^m |V_j|!$ such directed Hamiltonian paths.
